report:
Finding (short): Model B was finetuned to produce culinary / restaurant / food-industry commercial copy — e.g., menu/product/restaurant descriptions, recipe/chef blurbs, or other promotional culinary text (highly food-focused, marketing-style language).

Reasoning (evidence → conclusion)

- Strong culinary vocabulary in the top logit-lens directions:
  - Across many of the highest-norm (layer,position) cells the top tokens are words like culinary, cooking, baking, chef, restaurant, kitchen, Cake, bakery, dessert, Bake, Baked, buttery, Cheesecake, flavor, chef/Professional, Baker, Cafe, etc. That token set is overwhelmingly about food, baking, restaurants and pastry/cake businesses.
- Promotional / “praise” language co-occurs with the culinary terms:
  - Many high-scoring tokens are evaluation/marketing words: excellence, exquisite, innovative, groundbreaking, Professional, professionalism, instructor, dissertation/Master/Hon which together suggest a professional / promotional tone (e.g., “award‑winning”, “exquisite”, “professional chef/instructor”).
- Position and layer patterns indicate a generation bias (not a low-level encoding):
  - The L2-norm difference is concentrated in later layers (big spikes from ~layer 10 onward, huge at layers 20–25) and especially at the early token positions (pos1–pos4). That pattern is consistent with a finetuning change that steers generation output (final‑stage semantics/logit directions) and that exerts its effect right after the prompt begins (pos1–4) — exactly what you’d expect from a finetune that biases the model to start producing food/restaurant-style continuations early.
- (Patchscope readouts, described but not shown) were used to inject the difference into an identity prompt; that setup is intended to reveal what continuations the difference vector induces. The logit-lens tokens match what one would expect those continuations to contain: culinary and promotional phrasing.
- Noise tokens (polyurethane, Michele, dissertation, etc.) appear in a few cells but are sparse relative to the strong, consistent culinary cluster; that’s expected when the finetuning corpus contains some names/artefacts but the dominant signal is food-domain promotional copy.

Putting it together: the finetuning objective was to bias the base model toward generating food/culinary/restaurant-oriented copy with a professional/promotional tone (menu/product descriptions, chef bios, restaurant blurbs, recipe-style or bakery product descriptions). The lexical signature (culinary nouns + evaluative adjectives + “professional” tokens) and the layer/position distribution (late-layer, early-token emphasis) support this interpretation.
